title: Saying no
goal: Negate anything correctly — and accept the strangest fact about Finnish: the word "not" is a verb, and it changes with the subject.
bekal: build the six forms of the negative verb *ei* and pair them with the verb stem
negate *olla* and *minulla on*, together with the partitive that must go with them
say no, apologize, and admit you don't understand without sounding rude

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Väärinkäsitys
dialogs.intro: In a campus corridor. Marek thinks Budi is coming to a weekend trip; it turns out he isn't.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Hei Budi! Tuletko sinä mökille lauantaina?
lines.id: Hi Budi! Are you coming to the cottage on Saturday?
lines.literal: hi Budi! come-? you to-cottage on-Saturday?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Sorry, I don't understand. Could you repeat that?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.id: On Saturday. To the cottage. On the lakeshore.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ai, nyt ymmärrän! Mutta en voi tulla. Minulla ei ole aikaa.
lines.id: Oh, now I get it! But I can't come. I don't have time.
lines.literal: ah, now understand-I! but not-I can come. at-me not is time-some.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minä teen töitä lauantaina. Enkä minä osaa uida.
lines.id: I'm working on Saturday. And I can't swim, either.
lines.literal: I make work-plural-some on-Saturday. and-not-I know-how swim.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Se ei ole ongelma! Me emme ui, me saunomme.
lines.id: That's not a problem! We don't swim, we take a sauna.
lines.literal: it not is problem! we not-we swim, we sauna.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Saunotteko te talvella? Eikö se ole kylmää?
lines.id: You do sauna in winter? Isn't it cold?
lines.literal: sauna-you-? you in-winter? not-?-it is cold-some?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Sauna ei ole kylmä. Järvi on kylmä!
lines.id: The sauna isn't cold. The lake is cold!
lines.literal: sauna not is cold. lake is cold!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voi ei. Te ette ole normaaleja.
lines.id: Oh no. You people aren't normal.
lines.literal: oh no. you not-you are normal-plural-some.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Suomalaiset eivät ole normaaleja. Se on totta!
lines.literal: Finn-plural not-they are normal-plural-some. it is true.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ehkä ensi kerralla. Mutta en lupaa mitään!
lines.id: Maybe next time. But I'm not promising anything!

notes: **Ei is a verb, and it carries the subject.** This is the hardest part of the unit. In *en ymmärrä*, the word that says "I" isn't *ymmärrä* but *en*. The main verb is left bare — no person ending at all. English "not" never changes; Finnish treats it as a full verb.

**The main verb goes into its bare form.** *Ymmärrän → en ymmärrä*, *voin → en voi*, *tulen → en tule*, *olen → en ole*. What is left is the stem with no ending. That makes negation actually **easier** than a plain sentence — once you know the six forms of *ei*, the rest is just cutting off endings.

**Etkö? — questions can be negative too.** The question ending *-kö* attaches to the negative verb: *etkö* (don't you), *eikö* (doesn't he/it), *emmekö* (don't we). To answer: *En.* / *Kyllä.* Note that *kyllä* here means "oh yes I do" — it contradicts the negative, like German *doch*.

**Enkä** = *en* + *-kä* ("and not"). When one negative sentence is joined to another, *ja* is replaced by the ending *-kä*: *enkä minä osaa uida* (and I can't swim either). The forms: *enkä, etkä, eikä, emmekä, ettekä, eivätkä*.

**Minulla ei ole aikaa** — the thing must take the partitive. The positive sentence is *minulla on aika*; once negated, *aika* becomes *aikaa*. This isn't optional: negation **always** puts the negated thing in the partitive. *En juo kahvi**a***, *en syö liha**a***, *minulla ei ole auto**a***.

**Se ei ole ongelma, but Te ette ole normaaleja.** Why isn't the first one in the partitive? Because *ongelma* here names a **kind**, not an amount — and an adjective describing a plural subject always takes the plural partitive (*normaaleja*). The difference is subtle; at A1, just remember the *ei ole + noun* pattern as it appears in the dialogue.

grammars.title: Ei — the negative word that changes
body: Six forms you really must know by heart, because they appear in every negative sentence you will ever say in Finnish.
after: Notice that the verb columns **don't change at all** from top to bottom. The whole job of marking the person is taken over by the negative verb. It is a big saving that beginners rarely notice.
**The bare form is the same as the command form.** *Puhu!* (speak!) and *en puhu* use exactly the same form. So if you know how to give an order, you know how to negate — and vice versa.

⚠️ The bare form uses the **weak grade**: *lukea → luen → en lue*, *ottaa → otan → en ota*, *mennä → menen → en mene*. The practical shortcut: take the *minä* form and drop the *-n*. That is almost always right.

grammars.title: Negation demands the partitive
body: The unit's second rule, and it has no exceptions: **whatever is negated changes to the partitive.** That is why a positive sentence and its negative never look like a neat pair.
after: The last row shows something comforting: if the positive sentence is **already** in the partitive (as language names are), the negative changes nothing. This happens more often than you'd think.
⚠️ What does **not** change is the subject. *Minä en ole opiskelija* — *minä* stays *minä*. Only the object or the thing owned goes into the partitive.

If you forget to change it, you'll still be understood — but you'll sound exactly like a foreigner who has just started, and it is one of the mistakes Finnish ears catch fastest. Practice the pairs together: every time you learn a new sentence, learn its negative too.

sections.title: Saying no and admitting you don't know

blocks.text: Saying no in Finnish doesn't call for long pleasantries. A direct answer is considered honest and polite, not rude — but adding one short reason still makes it warmer.

head: Suomi
Say it
English
rows: I can't (I'm not able to make it).
That won't work; that doesn't suit me.

blocks.title: Osata or voida?
items: **Osata** = to have the skill. *En osaa uida* — I can't swim (I never learned).
**Voida** = to have the opportunity. *En voi tulla* — I can't come (something is in the way).
**Saada** = to have permission. *En saa tulla* — I'm not allowed to come.
English uses "can" for all three, so this distinction is genuinely new. Picking the wrong one changes what your sentence means, not just its tone.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **The negative verb is still required.** *Kukaan ei tiedä* uses *ei* even though *kukaan* on its own already means "nobody". Finnish negates twice — something standard English forbids ("nobody doesn't know"), but in Finnish it is the only correct way.
*Ei enää* and *ei vielä* come as a pair and are often mixed up. The rule of thumb: *vielä* looks forward (not yet, but maybe later), *enää* looks back (it used to be, but no longer).

blocks.title: The one sentence you'll need most
items: *Anteeksi, en ymmärrä. Voitko puhua hitaammin?* — "Sorry, I don't understand. Could you speak more slowly?"
Nobody is offended by it, and it is far better than nodding along pretending to understand — a habit that is very hard to shake and only slows your learning down.

exercises.prompt: Make these negative. Remember the partitive.

items: Hän ____ soittaa pianoa. (doesn't have the skill)
Me ____ auttaa tänään. (something in the way)

answers: Minä en ymmärrä suomea. — Sinä et tule lauantaina. — Hän ei ole opiskelija. — Me emme ole Helsingissä. — Te ette puhu englantia. — He eivät tiedä sitä.
Minulla ei ole autoa. — Minulla ei ole aikaa. — En juo kahvia. — En syö leipää. — Meillä ei ole lapsia. — En osta kirjaa.
En ymmärrä. — Minulla ei ole aikaa. — En osaa uida. — Se ei ole ongelma. — Miksi et? — En lupaa mitään.
En osaa — En voi — En saa — ei osaa — emme voi
